extracted.intended_audience: readers of entertainment industry news; comedy club owners, performers, and the general public interested in platforming debates
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and on-the-ground standards for comedy-club owners and programmers about whether and how to host comedians accused of misconduct — covering notification, presentation, principle of platforming, staff/peer impact, and practical risk management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambushing the audience / provide advance notice
rubrics_metrics.description: “The ambush is a real issue… I need to think about how to handle that in the future.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not put patrons in a position of feeling like a captive audience; give advance notice of controversial performers, announce shows so attendees know who is appearing, and consider explicitly warning or offering options. The owner suggested announced shows where “everybody came in knew that Louis C.K.’s coming” and that the first five minutes should be treated with gravity so the performer doesn’t appear dismissive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow platforming on principle of free expression (be a platform)
rubrics_metrics.description: “On principle, I believe that the man is entitled to his livelihood and that it’s up to the audience to go or not go… I would just like to be a platform.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate allowing a performance from endorsing a performer’s character or actions. Venue operators may choose to prioritize free-expression/platforming principles while recognizing that letting someone perform is not an endorsement — but must weigh reputational and practical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer should address allegations / offer contrition when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: “What he didn’t do is that he didn’t go on and address the issue — he just went on and did a regular set. And I think that was a missed opportunity… if he had just said something that showed a different side of him, I think the headlines today would be much gentler.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a performer with recent serious allegations returns to a stage, it is recommended they acknowledge or address the matter in a considered way (especially in opening minutes) to meet audience expectations and reduce backlash; failing to do so can be framed as dismissive and worsen reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh whether the booking benefits the venue or is merely a downside
rubrics_metrics.description: “This is nothing but a difficulty for us — there’s no benefit here for us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tangible and reputational benefits versus costs before booking controversial figures. Avoid decisions that create problems for staff, patrons, or the club without clear upside; do not rely on hidden payments as justification (owner denied payment and framed it as not helpful to the club).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider impact on other performers (perceived endorsement risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: “If he goes up then them appearing with him will be read as an endorsement of him and if so that it could damage them… many female comics… take this issue very seriously.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult and consider how other performers — especially those who may be vulnerable or who worked with accusers — will be affected; recognize that sharing a bill can be perceived as endorsement and have career consequences for peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid acting as judge or jury without due process
rubrics_metrics.description: “Before you know it, it becomes the automatic responsibility… that the guy who owns the comedy club is supposed to decide what happened, who’s guilty, what the punishment is… I don’t want to be judge or jury — I don’t really know anything.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venue decisions should account for limits of the owner/manager’s information and investigative rights. Don’t create policies that require the promoter to resolve contested factual claims absent fair procedures; beware of inconsistent or ad-hoc punishment standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer not to be the first stop in a comeback (timing/positioning)</description>
rubrics_metrics.description: “No, I don’t prefer to be the first stop; I wish I would be the last stop.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider timing: hosting an embattled performer early in their comeback increases scrutiny and risk. Some venues may choose to avoid being the first to reintroduce a controversial figure and instead wait until public sentiment or context changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat comeback appearances with appropriate presentation and framing
rubrics_metrics.description: “I would want to have announced shows where everybody came in knew that Louis C.K.’s coming. I would have [wanted him to] treat it with a certain gravity. That first five minutes I think really needed to have a lot of thought.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the event (ticketing, marketing copy, stage introduction, and the performer’s opening remarks) to acknowledge the context; deliberate presentation can mitigate perceptions of dismissiveness and show respect for affected audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit and respond to customer complaints and communicate with upset patrons
rubrics_metrics.description: “I apologize because I take absolute liability for any unhappy customer… I invited him to come back and to meet me.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have a clear customer-relations plan: acknowledge complaints, offer to meet or remedy, apologize if patrons feel ambushed, and use feedback to adjust future policies (e.g., advance-notice procedures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply consistent standards and consider precedent across cases
rubrics_metrics.description: “I don’t think anyone’s come after the theaters and stages that allow Mike Tyson to tour…the Aziz thing is a great example, because who the hell knows what went on there?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developable policies should be coherent across different types of allegations and figures to avoid arbitrary distinctions; compare similar cases to justify decisions and be aware of public inconsistencies that will be scrutinized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance artist livelihood and the unique nature of stand-up as audience-dependent art
rubrics_metrics.description: “For a stand-up comedian…for the world to think, ‘You shall not have an audience again…’ it is similar in a way to ‘We think your punishment should be that you shall never pick up a paintbrush again’ for an artist.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that preventing a performer from working entirely is especially consequential for stand-ups, whose craft depends on live audiences; weigh rehabilitative or restorative approaches versus permanent exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect staff and workplace safety / enforce internal harassment-avoidance rules
rubrics_metrics.description: “I’ve always been ahead of the curve in empowering my female employees to not have to [deal with harassment]… 20 or 25 years ago I had a rule that no male could give a female a back rub because I understood the creepy dynamic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain and enforce workplace policies to protect employees and create a safe working environment independent of booking decisions; ensure staff concerns are considered when deciding whom to host.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gauge audience composition and sentiment when evaluating bookings
rubrics_metrics.description: “It’s around 50/50 [gender].” “I’ve so far received only one complaint…we had four or five positive emails.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess likely audience demographics and collect pre- and post-show feedback to inform decisions; a small number of complaints versus many positive responses should be contextualized rather than taken as sole justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage public conversation and nuanced discourse rather than immediate condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: “We’re living in the dark ages of people having things they believe that they know they can’t say out loud… Conversation in this day and age is just for two people to agree to talk about what they agree about.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where appropriate, foster mechanisms (panels, discussions, moderated talks) that allow for nuanced conversation about allegations, accountability, and redemption, while recognizing power imbalances and victims’ perspectives.
